citation: Wiesmann T, Müller S, Müller HH, Wulf H, Steinfeldt T. Effect of bupivacaine and adjuvant drugs for regional anesthesia on nerve tissue oximetry and nerve blood flow. J Pain Res 2018;11:227-235
text_quality: ok (9 PDF pages, reading-order text complete; the rotated Tables 2-4 on PDF pages 6-7 are scrambled in the text and were read from rendered page images). Author list on PDF page 1 matches the given list. Free full text also in PMC (PMC5789040).
design: Randomised controlled animal experiment, four parallel groups: one median nerve per brachial plexus was randomly assigned to one topically applied test solution; exclusion decisions on the recordings were made blinded to group; reported to ARRIVE guidelines; sample size calculated for nerve blood flow at 60 min.
population: Healthy anaesthetised, paralysed and mechanically ventilated pigs (28 pigs; 56 median nerves exposed). The median nerve was surgically exposed in the axilla (axillary brachial plexus) with its extrinsic epineural vessels preserved. No neuropathy model.
n: 40 nerves analysed, n = 10 per group (saline, bupivacaine, bupivacaine with epinephrine, bupivacaine with clonidine). 16 nerves excluded: 6 before randomisation (probe mounting difficulty or surgical training), 3 for suspected injury to the extrinsic nerve vessels, 7 for probe dislocation / non-continuous recording.
setting: Laboratory animal study, University Hospital Marburg (Philipps University) and Giessen, Germany; general anaesthesia with propofol and sufentanil, fixed inspired oxygen fraction, normocapnia by capnometry, invasive arterial pressure monitored; animals euthanised at the end of the experiment.
intervention: One test solution per nerve, a single application of 1 mL dripped onto the surgically exposed median nerve next to the probe (spreading under the probe by capillary action), immediately after the T0 reading. Groups: bupivacaine [dose figure omitted] alone (Carbostesin, B. Braun); bupivacaine [dose figure omitted] with epinephrine 1:100,000 (Suprarenin, Sanofi-Aventis); bupivacaine [dose figure omitted] with clonidine [dose figure omitted] (Clonidin-ratiopharm). Freshly prepared from preservative-free single-dose vials. The epinephrine concentration is higher than (not the same as) the concentration named in claim C074. No epinephrine-alone or clonidine-alone arm; no dexamethasone; no lidocaine.
comparator: Normal saline (negative control, statistically compared only with bupivacaine); bupivacaine alone was the standard group against which each adjuvant group was compared (Mann-Whitney, Bonferroni-adjusted closed testing; Hodges-Lehmann estimates with 95% CI). Descriptive post hoc comparisons of saline versus each group.
route: Topical (extraneural) application onto the epineurium of a surgically exposed nerve. Not an injection: not intraneural, not a needle-placed perineural block, not intradermal.
duration: Single application; recordings at T0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50 and 60 min after a 10-min settling period; no recovery or follow-up (no histology, no electrophysiology, no later time points).
outcomes: Nerve blood flow by laser-Doppler flowmetry (relative to each nerve's baseline); nerve tissue oxygen saturation (SO2, %) of the capillary/post-capillary bed and relative tissue haemoglobin (rHb, arbitrary units, a marker of venous congestion) by white-light tissue spectrophotometry; flow, SO2 and rHb came from one combined O2C probe (LEA Medizintechnik) sampling about 1-2 mm deep inside the nerve; heart rate, mean arterial pressure and SpO2 at T0/T30/T60. Pre-specified order: relative flow T60, SO2 T60, rHb T60, then the same at T30. Results by direction (Tables 2-5, PDF pages 5-7): bupivacaine alone lowered nerve blood flow progressively (median about a third of baseline at 60 min; significantly below saline at 30 and 60 min) and lowered SO2 late (significantly below saline at 60 min); adding epinephrine made flow fall faster in the first 10-15 min but flow at 30 and 60 min did not differ significantly from bupivacaine alone; in the epinephrine group median SO2 was the lowest of the four groups from 5 to 30 min (74% at 10 min) and recovered to 91% by 60 min, with two nerves severely desaturated (nadirs 3% and 10%); SO2 with epinephrine did not differ significantly from bupivacaine alone at 30 or 60 min, nor from saline at 60 min; adding clonidine changed neither flow nor SO2 compared with bupivacaine alone; rHb did not differ between any groups; systemic vital signs did not differ relevantly. Internal inconsistency: the first paragraph of the Discussion (PDF page 5) says there was no significant SO2 difference between bupivacaine and saline, while the Results (p = 0.0005 at 60 min), Table 5 (p = 0.003) and the abstract report one.

key_results.quote: Combined tissue spectrophotometry and laser-Doppler flowmetry were used to assess nerve blood flow in 40 surgically exposed median nerves in pigs, as well as nerve tissue oximetry for 60 min.

Bupivacaine resulted in significant decrease in nerve blood flow, as well as tissue oximetry values, compared with saline control. Addition of epinephrine resulted in a rapid, but nonsignificant, reduction of nerve blood flow and extensive lowering of tissue oximetry levels.

The application of bupivacaine results in lower nerve blood flow, but does not induce relevant ischemia. Despite significant reductions in nerve blood flow, the addition of clonidine or epinephrine to bupivacaine had no significant impact on nerve tissue oximetry compared with bupivacaine alone.

Using the Mann–Whitney test, the bupivacaine group (standard group) showed a significant decrease of flow, compared with the saline group (control group) at T30 and T60 (both p < 0.0001), but was not significantly different from bupivacaine with added clonidine (T30, p = 1.0; T60, p = 0.19), or with added epinephrine (T30, p = 0.48; T60, p = 0.39).

No significant differences between the groups were found when comparing bupivacaine with saline at T0 (p = 0.472) and T30 (p = 0.623), whereas differences between both groups at T60 showed a significant difference (p = 0.0005).
Comparison of the SO2 values of the bupivacaine group with those of the BupiEpi group showed no significant differences at T0 (p = 0.382), T30 (p = 0.544), or T60 (p = 0.130).
No significant differences of rHb were found when comparing bupivacaine with the saline control at the time points T0 (p = 0.212), T30 (p = 0.226),

However, two nerves of the BupiEpi group did have relevant desaturations during measurements (SO2 nadir values of 3% at T20 and 10% at T10 in another nerve). Thus, despite no significant difference between both groups of bupivacaine, with and without epinephrine, we would recommend not to use epinephrine in a patient population with preexisting peripheral nerve damage (i.e., diabetic polyneuropathy).
No further alterations of nerve microcirculation or tissue oximetry were observed, compared with bupivacaine alone.
However, bupivacaine does show a relevant depression of nerve blood flow without resulting in severe nerve tissue ischemia.

author_limitations.quote: First, the differences between the results in this animal study might not be easily extrapolated to humans, due to possible differences in nerve blood flow and underlying regulative mechanisms between pigs and humans.
Changes in vascular tone might be influenced by general anesthesia, the surgical preparation
Furthermore, our investigation focused only on median nerves, but potential differences between nerve vasculature must be regarded.

Our measurements were performed for 60 min, which is higher than in previous studies. Nevertheless, the vasoconstrictive effects of the test solutions persisted for longer time periods. Further studies should evaluate this aspect using long-term measurements and include histological or electrophysiological evaluation.
Neurotoxicity of local anesthetics is not caused solely by ischemia as a result of reduced tissue perfusion.
